questions.question: What's the main reason to avoid using a named human user's password for a server-to-server integration?
options: It's technically impossible to use a human login for automation
It breaks the moment that person changes their password or leaves the company
It makes callouts run slower
Salesforce blocks this automatically in every org
questions.explanation: A dedicated integration user with a proper OAuth flow (JWT Bearer, Client Credentials) is stable and doesn't depend on one person's account lifecycle.

questions.question: Why is "callout failed" alone a weak log message for a failed integration?
options: It isn't weak; any log entry is equally useful
Log messages longer than a few words aren't supported in Apex
It doesn't give enough context (endpoint, status code, safe payload summary) to debug without reproducing it live
Salesforce automatically expands short log messages with more detail
questions.explanation: Useful failure logs capture enough context to diagnose the issue without having to reproduce it.

questions.question: What's the risk of configuring alerts for every possible event, including minor/expected ones?
options: There is no risk, more alerts are always better
Salesforce limits orgs to 10 alerts per day
Noisy alerting trains people to ignore it, so alerts that actually matter get missed
Over-alerting automatically escalates to Salesforce Support
questions.explanation: Alert fatigue is real — tune alerts to things that need action so the signal doesn't get lost in noise.

questions.question: Why should an integration user's permission set be scoped tightly rather than given broad access "just in case"?
options: Tight scoping makes callouts run measurably faster
Salesforce requires minimal permission sets by policy for every integration user
It has no security benefit, only a cosmetic one
It limits the blast radius if that credential is ever compromised
questions.explanation: Least-privilege access means a leaked credential exposes only what that integration actually needed — not the whole org.

questions.question: What should happen to an integration user's credentials once an integration project is decommissioned?
options: Leave them active indefinitely in case the integration is needed again someday
Nothing, decommissioned integrations pose no risk
Convert the user to System Administrator for safekeeping
Deactivate or tightly re-scope them — unused access left active is unmonitored risk
questions.explanation: Stale, forgotten credentials with standing access are a common source of risk — clean them up when the integration they supported is gone.
